rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Turn 3 Game End 4 Variations Overview Place a single counter each turn until you create one of the winning formations before your opponent does Turn On your turn, place your piece on any empty field Game End The game can end in 4 ways You win if you connect 3 fields of the same colour together, orthogonally or diagonally You win if you create a square of 4 connected fields regardless of colour You win if you create a line (orthogonal or diagonal) of 5 connected fields regardless of colour The game is a draw if the final counter is played and no winning formation is found Variations The basic game is Qango 6, the following are additional rules which can be implemented to vary complexity, the order of these generally represents the increasing difficulty they pose Castle - There are 8 spaces which form a castle-like formation which cannot be used by the first counter, but otherwise are free to use from 2nd turn onwards Tournament - The 1st counter can only be played from an edge space Quango 7 - There is a central yellow square which is unconnected to any yellows, thus cannot be used to win via method 1 Quango 7 Castle - This has a slightly different layout for the blocked opening squares Quango 7 and the First Professional - The first counter can only start on an edge or the central yellow space Quango 7 and the Second Professional - The first counter can only start on an edge but not the central space of each line Quango 7 Plus - The grey corner fields are banned for the whole game Quango 7 Plus and the Edge - The first counter can only be played on an edge space (as Grey is Banned, spaces next to Grey are the edge as well as true edge spaces) Quango 7 Plus and the Tournament - The first counter can only be played on either pair of green and blue spaces on opposite corners.

---

QANGO is an abstract two-player game that plays quickly and is explained even faster.

Players place their discs on a square multicolored board and try to either get three of their discs in one group of the same color, four discs in a square, or five discs in a horizontal, vertical or diagonal row to immediately win the game. They place one disc at a time and aren't limited in how to place the disc after the first move.

The game includes two boards, a beginner board with 6x6 squares and an advanced board with 7x7 squares.
community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] WTF is that... where is the game here? Starting move has to be countered what means choice between 2 moves just to not let the other player win... If we were taught proper rules at Essen, this game doesn't make any sense.

[Rating: 1/10] After 12 plays, we failed to find even the remotest hope for the second player to win.

[Rating: 1/10] Gave this a shot on yucata. When second you must choose from just two squares, it seems like there is a mammoth first player advantage.

[Rating: 2/10] Bigger tic-tac-toe. Not sure if the game is entirely solved but first player has such a huge advantage that, even if it isn't, it doesn't seem worth playing. Pretty board, at least.

[Rating: 2/10] on BGA, extreme tic-tac-toe gameplay: where one player forces the other to make moves to keep them from winning, over and over until they end in a tie. Yuck

[Rating: 3/10] Played at Spiel. First player plays, second player counters, first player plays, second player counters,..., first player wins. We played 3 times and 3 times it went like this.

[Rating: 3/10] Almost as bad as tic tac toe. It seems impossible to win if you’re not starting player.   [i]Played at Zuiderspel 2022.[/i]

[Rating: 3/10] There's a forced win in 4-5 moves for the first player. Really no need to play it.  Redeeming feature: I noticed that I had a guaranteed win after a few moves, and felt very clever until I learned that the game more or less set it up for me, rather than me having created it for myself.

[Rating: 3/10] This feels very tic-tac-toe-ish. There are a lot of forced moves since it's easy to occupy 2 adjacent squares of the same color. If players aren't thinking ahead, you could fill most of the board this way, which doesn't make for an exciting game.  The rules only list limitations for the first player under recommendations for stronger players: the base rules don't limit the first move. That's why so many reviews are complaining of a first-player advantage.  I did not find this interesting.  See my thoughts about other 2-player combinatorial abstracts in my [geeklist=361723][color=#005bca]2-play

[Rating: 4/10] An abstract I'm not that keen to play again, but in a way curious if it's easily solvable.

[Rating: 4/10] Boring shallow unoriginal game. How much can this be played before becoming terribly repetitive?
